strengths: Proposes PvP, a simple and intuitive contrastive learning framework that leverages proprioceptive-privileged state complementarity to learn compact latent representations for humanoid whole-body control without standard hand-crafted data augmentations.

Introduces SRL4Humanoid, a modular and unified framework implementing representative state representation learning methods (VAE, SPR, SimSiam) alongside PvP, enabling systematic comparison and future benchmarking.

Conducts extensive simulation experiments on the LimX Oli humanoid robot across velocity tracking and motion imitation tasks, including ablations on update interval, data proportion, and applying SRL to policy vs. value encoders.

Demonstrates promising empirical results: PvP substantially accelerates learning on the velocity tracking task and achieves the highest tracking performance on motion imitation KPIs, with qualitative real-world deployment on the physical robot.
Provides detailed reproducibility material in the supplementary, including network architectures, PPO hyperparameters, reward formulations, and state specifications.
weaknesses: Serious technical inconsistency in state definitions: the proprioceptive state is described as 5-frame stacked (e.g., 535 dimensions for velocity tracking), while the privileged state is specified without stacking (110 dimensions). The claimed relation o ⊂ s and the zero-masking operation ̃s = ZeroMasking(s) therefore cannot produce matched paired views as described, undermining the core contrastive learning setup.

Unclear how the policy encoder is trained on privileged state s and zero-masked s while the deployed policy network accepts proprioceptive state o. The input dimensions, history length, and deployment-time input distribution are not reconciled, making the method's implementation ambiguous.

No comparison to established privileged learning baselines such as asymmetric actor-critic, teacher-student distillation, or learning-by-cheating, despite PvP explicitly using privileged information. The claim of outperforming existing SRL baselines is therefore narrow.

Real-world evaluation is qualitative only (screenshots and video references). No quantitative real-world success rates, tracking errors, or baseline comparisons are reported, yet the paper claims real-world deployment reliability.
Computational efficiency claims are not quantitatively supported in the paper; no wall-clock time, GPU memory, or training-time comparisons are provided, only a reference to external Wandb logs.

Statistical significance is not assessed. Improvements on motion imitation are modest and confidence intervals appear to overlap in some comparisons, so the strength of the claims is not fully established.
The paper is a state-based robot learning/RL contribution with no visual perception or computer vision component, making it arguably out of scope for CVPR.

Ablations are incomplete: no study of alternative privileged information choices, masking strategies, predictor design, or stop-gradient necessity. The interval update mechanism (Eq. 6) is heuristic and not theoretically justified.
The claim of avoiding hand-crafted data augmentations is overstated: zero-masking is itself a hand-crafted operation, and the selection of privileged state components is manually designed.

strengths: Addresses an important problem: sample inefficiency in humanoid whole-body control RL, where high-dimensional dynamics and partial observability make learning costly.

Proposes a simple and practical plug-and-play method, PvP, that uses privileged-state zero-masking as a pseudo-augmentation and applies SimSiam-style contrastive learning between proprioceptive and privileged representations, avoiding hand-crafted augmentations and integrating easily with PPO.

Provides a systematic empirical study on a full-size LimX Oli humanoid robot across two representative tasks (velocity tracking and motion imitation), comparing against PPO, PPO+VAE, PPO+SPR, and PPO+SimSiam, with multiple ablations on update intervals, training-data proportion, encoder target, and computational efficiency.

Introduces SRL4Humanoid, a unified and modular framework for state-representation learning in humanoid RL, with implementations of representative SRL methods; the supplementary material supplies architecture, hyperparameter, reward, and state-definition details, supporting reproducibility.

Reports several useful practical insights: interval SRL updates can avoid premature convergence; applying SRL to the policy encoder is more stable than applying it to the value encoder; and suitable update intervals/data proportions can improve performance.
The paper is generally clear, well organized, and supported by learning curves, bar charts, and qualitative deployment images.
Real-world and Sim2Sim demonstrations, while qualitative, provide initial evidence that the learned policies can be deployed beyond simulation.
weaknesses: Methodological novelty is moderate: the core idea is a straightforward combination of existing ingredients (privileged state, zero-masking, SimSiam-style contrastive learning, PPO). The paper does not provide theoretical analysis or deeper insight into why the proposed contrastive objective improves policy learning.
Evaluation breadth is limited to one humanoid platform (LimX Oli) and two tasks. More diverse robot morphologies, terrains, and dynamic behaviors would strengthen the generality claims.

Real-world evaluation is essentially qualitative: Figure 1 and Figure 11 show snapshots/Sim2Sim rollouts, but no quantitative real-robot success rates, tracking errors, or reliability metrics are reported, despite real-world deployment being a stated claim.

The comparison omits standard privileged learning / asymmetric actor-critic / teacher-student baselines and closely related methods such as PIM, which is discussed in related work but not benchmarked. This makes it difficult to establish the advantage of PvP over existing privileged-learning alternatives.

Experimental rigor details are incomplete: the number of random seeds and any statistical significance tests are not reported, the sensitivity to the SRL loss weight λ is not ablated in the main paper, and the update interval T appears heuristically chosen.

There is an inconsistency in the degree-of-freedom labels: the text refers to LimX-Oli-31dof tasks while multiple figures use LimX-Oli-32dof; Figure 4 lists 31 active DoF. This should be corrected for clarity.

The claimed computational efficiency is not substantiated with quantitative wall-clock, GPU-memory, or throughput comparisons in the manuscript; the reader is referred to external W&B logs, which may not be accessible.
The paper states that SRL4Humanoid is open-source, but no code repository or URL is provided in the manuscript, weakening reproducibility and community-use claims.

It is not fully isolated whether gains come from the contrastive objective itself, from the availability of privileged information, or from the zero-masking/padding scheme; representation-quality analyses such as linear probing or collapse metrics are absent.
The action smoothness result is a simulation reward term, not a real-world safety/reliability metric; using it as direct evidence of real-world deployment reliability is somewhat overclaimed.

strengths: Addresses a genuinely important problem: sample-efficient whole-body control (WBC) for humanoid robots, where RL sample complexity is a well-recognized bottleneck.

The proposed PvP method is conceptually reasonable: leveraging the intrinsic complementarity between proprioceptive and privileged states via a SimSiam-style contrastive objective is a sensible and simple design that does not require hand-crafted augmentations.

The SRL4Humanoid framework, which provides unified and modular implementations of representative SRL methods (VAE, SPR, SimSiam) on top of PPO, could be a useful engineering resource for the community and supports reproducibility.

The empirical study is relatively broad, including ablations on update interval, data proportion, policy-vs-value encoder placement, and computational cost, which goes beyond a single headline number.
The manuscript is generally clear, well-organized, and the figures (especially Figure 1 and Figure 5) communicate the motivation and main trends effectively.
A real-world deployment on the LimX Oli robot is shown, which adds practical relevance.
weaknesses: Limited novelty. Both privileged-information learning (asymmetric actor-critic, teacher-student distillation, privileged learning) and contrastive representation learning for RL are long-established ideas. The specific combination proposed here (contrastive alignment between a proprioceptive state and a zero-masked privileged state) is an incremental instantiation rather than a new conceptual contribution.

The most directly relevant baselines are missing. Since PvP is fundamentally a privileged-information method, the natural comparisons are asymmetric actor-critic and teacher-student privileged distillation approaches; instead, the only baselines are PPO augmented with generic SRL objectives (VAE, SPR, SimSiam), which weakens the evidence that PvP is better than existing privileged-learning alternatives.

The zero-masking formulation is crude and under-justified. Because the privileged state s contains the proprioceptive state o as a subset, ZeroMasking(s) is essentially o padded with zeros; it is not clear why this is a good 'augmentation' or why the encoder can meaningfully process inputs of different dimensionality. The paper does not analyze whether the learned representation actually encodes privileged information or simply learns to ignore it.

The empirical gains are uneven and task-dependent. In Figure 5, PvP is clearly best for velocity tracking, but for motion imitation the improvements over vanilla PPO are marginal and SimSiam/SPR are competitive. The abstract's broad claim of 'significantly improves sample efficiency and final performance' is not uniformly supported by the evidence.

Real-world evaluation is thin. Section 5.2.6 is very short, and the main quantitative real-world evidence (Figure 11) is Sim2Sim evaluation on MuJoCo rather than hardware experiments. The hardware results in Figure 1 are largely qualitative and lack quantitative metrics, so the claim of reliable real-world deployment is not strongly substantiated.

The contribution of SRL4Humanoid is primarily engineering (a unified re-implementation of existing SRL methods) rather than a scientific advance; its 'first unified and modular framework' claim is difficult to verify and is not the kind of contribution that typically carries a top-tier vision/robotics paper on its own.
Evaluation is limited to a single robot (LimX Oli) and a single simulator (IsaacLab), so generalization across platforms, morphologies, and simulators is not demonstrated.

Several technical details are under-specified, e.g., how the dimension mismatch between o and s is handled in the shared-weight encoder, what 'identity mapping' contributes in Figure 2(b), and how the interval update mechanism was tuned (the choice T=50 appears heuristic and is only lightly ablated).

The interval-update mechanism (Eq. 6) is presented as a practical fix but is not analyzed theoretically; it is unclear whether the reported benefit stems from the SRL objective itself or from an implicit regularization schedule, which weakens the interpretability of the central claim.
Claims of 'significantly' better performance would benefit from statistical significance testing across seeds; only mean/std curves are reported.

strengths: The core idea is simple, intuitive, and practically effective: forming the positive view by zero-masking the privileged component of the state (Eq. 2) sidesteps hand-crafted augmentations and yields a real speedup. In velocity tracking (Fig. 5), PvP reaches ~0.9 normalized score by roughly 5k iterations while vanilla PPO and the VAE/SPR baselines need ~25k iterations, which is a substantial and clearly visible effect.

The empirical study is systematic and broad for a single paper: SRL objective placement on policy vs. value encoder (Fig. 10), update interval (Fig. 8), training-data proportion (Fig. 9), loss weighting lambda (Fig. 17), and a head-to-head comparison against teacher-student distillation (Figs. 13-14). These ablations produce concrete, actionable guidance (e.g., interval updates, lambda = 0.1, policy-encoder placement) rather than only headline numbers.

The SRL4Humanoid framework is a genuine community contribution: it decouples SRL from RL (Fig. 3) and provides matched network architectures and training budgets across VAE/SPR/SimSiam (Tables 5-6), which is what makes the cross-method comparison credible. Code is stated to be released, aiding reproducibility.

Validation on a real 31-DoF LimX Oli humanoid for both velocity tracking and motion imitation (Fig. 1c, Fig. 11, supplementary videos) is valuable and relatively uncommon in this literature, and the Sim2Sim MuJoCo check before hardware adds credibility.

The paper honestly identifies and addresses a practical failure mode of auxiliary SRL losses (premature convergence to local optima from low-quality early data) with the interval-update mechanism of Eq. 6, and reports the training collapse when SRL is applied to the value encoder (Fig. 10) instead of hiding it.
weaknesses: Methodological novelty is modest. PvP is essentially SimSiam [1] applied to a (privileged state, zero-masked privileged state) pair, where the 'augmentation' is just removal of the privileged subset. The ingredients (SimSiam predictor/stop-gradient, asymmetric actor-critic with a privileged critic, auxiliary representation losses in RL) are all pre-existing, and the paper does not provide deeper justification for why contrastive alignment between a set and its subset should specifically yield task-relevant features.

The central claim of 'compact and task-relevant latent representations' is asserted but never directly evidenced. There is no probing, latent-space visualization, dimensionality/information analysis, or any measurement of what the learned encoder actually encodes. The paper reports only downstream reward curves, so the representational story is unverified.

A key control baseline is missing: an auxiliary objective that directly predicts/regresses the privileged signal from proprioception (the natural non-contrastive alternative to PvP). Because VAE (reconstruction) and SPR (latent dynamics prediction) are compared but direct privileged prediction is not, the observed gains cannot be cleanly attributed to the contrastive structure rather than to simply injecting privileged supervision into the encoder. This is the ablation that would most strengthen the paper's causal claim.

Real-world evaluation is qualitative only. Figure 1c and Figure 11 are image sequences; there are no quantitative hardware metrics (tracking error, success/fall rates, energy, robustness to perturbation) and no baseline run on the robot. The abstract's claim about improving 'real-world deployment reliability' is therefore not fully supported by the reported evidence.

Evaluation breadth is limited: two tasks on essentially one platform (with a single additional Untreee-G1 curve in the appendix, Fig. 16). The selected privileged signal differs between tasks (root linear velocity for velocity tracking, plus orientation for mimicry, Appendix C.2) with no guidance on how to choose privileged variables for a new task, which limits the generality of the recipe.

The design choice that defines the method - zero-masking the privileged part to build the positive pair - is not isolated in an ablation. Other ways of forming the pair (random masking, temporal offsets, different masking ratios) are used for the SimSiam baseline but never systematically varied for PvP, so it is unclear how sensitive the method is to this specific construction.

Reporting details needed to judge significance are incomplete: the number of seeds is not stated, hyperparameter search procedures and results for the baselines (Appendices C.3-C.5) are described only as searched values with no sensitivity analysis, and some claims outrun the error bars (e.g., in Fig. 7 the PPO+PvP and PPO+SPR bars overlap on waist-pitch orientation and feet distance, while the text describes PvP as achieving 'the highest performance across the three key tracking metrics').

Fit with the venue is weak: the method operates purely on proprioceptive state with no visual input, and the paper itself lists RGB/depth integration as future work. As a robot-learning contribution this is reasonable, but as a CVPR submission the computer-vision relevance is thin.

strengths: Addresses an important problem: sample efficiency in humanoid whole-body control RL, where data efficiency remains a major bottleneck.

Proposes a simple and intuitive method, PvP, that uses the privileged simulator state as a positive pair for the proprioceptive state via SimSiam-style contrastive learning, avoiding hand-crafted augmentations and showing consistent improvements over PPO and SRL baselines (VAE, SPR, SimSiam) on velocity tracking and motion imitation (Figs. 5-7).

Introduces SRL4Humanoid, a unified and modular framework for representative SRL methods in humanoid RL, improving reproducibility and enabling systematic study of SRL design choices (Figs. 3, 8-10; Appendix).

Provides a thorough set of ablations: update intervals, training data proportion, policy vs. value encoder, lambda weighting, teacher-student distillation comparison, additional tasks (rough terrain and Unitree G1), and computational efficiency analysis (Figs. 8-10, 13-17).
Demonstrates real-world deployment on the LimX Oli humanoid and Sim2Sim evaluation in MuJoCo, supporting practical feasibility (Figs. 1, 11; supplementary videos).
The paper is generally well organized, with clear figures, tables, and algorithmic details; code is promised for reproducibility.
weaknesses: Scope/fit for CVPR is questionable: the method operates only on proprioceptive and privileged states, with no visual input, and is essentially a robot learning/RL contribution rather than a computer vision or pattern recognition advance; it may be better suited to robotics venues (CoRL/ICRA/RSS).

Methodological novelty is moderate: combining privileged information with contrastive learning (SimSiam) is a straightforward extension, and the paper does not provide theoretical analysis or a clear explanation of why the contrastive objective should learn useful task-relevant representations beyond empirical curves.

Real-world evaluation lacks quantitative metrics: only qualitative images/videos are shown, with no success rates, tracking errors, or statistical comparisons on the real robot, which weakens the deployment claims.

Some comparisons are potentially unfair or overstated: the teacher-student distillation (TSD) student fails to learn in both tasks (Figs. 13-14), which may reflect an implementation issue rather than a fundamental limitation of TSD; error bars overlap in some comparisons, making 'significant' claims less convincing (e.g., mimic task in Fig. 5 and KPIs in Fig. 7).

The interval update mechanism in Eq. (6) is heuristic and not well motivated: the choice of T is not principled, and the degradation from continuous SRL is not thoroughly explained, limiting practical guidance.

Clarity issues around zero-masking and dimension alignment: the paper does not fully specify how the same policy encoder processes differently sized proprioceptive and privileged states, and how the zero-masking is applied exactly (Section 4.1, Appendix C.2).

No statistical significance tests are reported, and the main text lacks a quantitative computational-cost table despite claiming efficiency; limitations and societal impact are only briefly mentioned.

strengths: The core idea is simple and clearly explained: use the privileged/proprioceptive split of the simulator state as the two views of a SimSiam-style contrastive objective, so that the policy encoder learns a latent space that predicts task-relevant privileged quantities from proprioception alone. The method is easy to implement on top of any PPO pipeline.

The paper releases SRL4Humanoid, a modular, decoupled implementation of representative state-representation-learning methods (PPO, PPO+VAE, PPO+SPR, PPO+SimSiam, PPO+PvP) for humanoid whole-body control, which is a genuinely useful engineering artifact for the community and supports the reproducibility claim (code link provided).

The empirical study is broad for a paper of this length: two tasks (velocity tracking, motion imitation), four SRL baselines, ablations on update interval, data proportion, encoder placement, loss weight, a comparison against teacher-student distillation, plus an extra robot (Unitree G1) and a rough-terrain variant, and a real-robot demonstration. The speed-up on velocity tracking is large and reproduces across the G1 and rough-terrain settings.

The paper reports negative/awkward results honestly (VAE degradation on the mimic task, training collapse when the SRL loss is applied to the value encoder), which is informative for practitioners and is not cherry-picked away.
weaknesses: The scientific contribution is thin for CVPR. The method is essentially SimSiam applied to two views defined by the privileged/proprioceptive split; contrastive and privileged-information learning for RL are both well established (CURL, ATC, SPR, RND-style intrinsic objectives, asymmetric actor-critic/teacher-student). The paper itself concedes that prior work such as PIM already applies contrastive learning to humanoid locomotion, and the delta over it is the addition of privileged information as a second view. The claimed novelty is incremental.

The claim that PvP works 'without requiring hand-crafted data augmentations' is contradicted by the method itself: the second view is constructed by zero-masking the privileged dimensions of the state (Eq. 2), which is precisely a hand-crafted, structure-dependent augmentation. What actually becomes hand-crafted is the per-task choice of which privileged variables to include (root linear velocity for velocity tracking, root orientation for mimic, Appendix C.2), so the design burden is shifted rather than removed.

A likely confound is not controlled for. In the velocity-tracking task the privileged signal is the robot's root linear velocity, i.e. exactly the quantity the reward is defined on. Training the encoder to be predictive of that variable is trivially aligned with the task, and the much smaller/overlapping gains on the mimic task (Fig. 5, Fig. 7) are consistent with this explanation. The paper never runs the obvious control: predicting the privileged state directly with an MSE/regression head, or simply feeding the privileged state to the policy/value network (asymmetric actor-critic). Without that ablation, the claim that the contrastive objective (rather than privileged-variable injection) causes the improvement is unsupported.

Key baselines are missing: (a) a privileged-state reconstruction/prediction baseline, which is the natural alternative to the contrastive objective and the paper's own stated target ('reconstruction-based approaches... struggle with suboptimal representation quality'); VAE reconstructing proprioception is not a substitute; (b) PIM [20], which is criticized in related work but never evaluated; (c) intrinsic-motivation SRL (RND/ICM) and other contrastive RL objectives. Only three SRL baselines are compared, and they are all tuned by an ad-hoc 'initial hyperparameter search' described only in the appendix.

Fairness of the main comparison is unclear with respect to the interval-update mechanism. Eq. (6) introduces an indicator that applies the SRL loss only every T steps, motivated by an asserted (but unverified) claim that the loss 'prematurely falls into local optima' early in training. Section 5.2.2 states that the SRL methods are updated synchronously by default, while Fig. 8 shows interval 50 is optimal for all methods. The paper never states which setting was used to produce Figs. 5–7, so it is impossible to tell whether PvP's advantage comes from the contrastive objective or from a more favorable update schedule. This must be disambiguated.

The real-world evidence is qualitative only. Fig. 1(c) shows a handful of frames and the text defers to a supplementary video; there are no success rates, trial counts, task metrics, or failure analysis on the physical LimX Oli. Claims such as 'guarantee the reliability of real-world deployment' and 'validate our approach on the LimX Oli humanoid robot' are therefore not supported by quantitative evidence.

Statistical support is weak. The number of seeds is not reported in the main text, no significance testing is performed, and in the mimic task (Fig. 5 right, Fig. 7) the PvP, SimSiam and SPR curves/error bars overlap substantially, yet the text describes the result as 'significantly' better. The abstract's claim of improved 'final performance' overstates what the mimic results show.

Venue fit: the paper contains no visual perception component whatsoever. All observations are proprioceptive/simulator state vectors and the related work, baselines and benchmarks are RL/robotics. The conclusion itself lists 'incorporating multimodal data such as RGB or depth images' as future work, confirming the absence of any vision contribution. This is a poor match for CVPR and reads as a robotics-venue (CoRL/ICRA/IROS) paper.

Secondary contributions are overclaimed. 'The first unified and modular open-source framework' for SRL in humanoid learning is unverifiable and is not the paper's scientific contribution; RSRL [32] and similar libraries already exist. Presentation also has inconsistencies (SRLAHumanoid vs SRL4Humanoid; IsaacLab cited as [23] and [25]; MuJoCo referred to as a 'platform' for Sim2Sim evaluation), and the argument that early massive-parallel low-quality data drives SRL to local optima is asserted rather than demonstrated.
